Asking rent and paid rent: read the population before setting your moving budget

Compare official Q2 2026 rent observations, inspect the asking-minus-paid difference and test an actual quote against the full household budget in four charts.

By TickerLantern Research · Published 25 October 2026 · 4 min read
Sources reviewed 25 October 2026

Change an assumption. Follow the result.

Explore an actual rent quote beside a complete monthly budget

Interactive planning lab

Rent, excluded utilities and tenant insurance each month$2,590
Housing plus location-specific transport each month$2,790
Monthly cash after living costs and saving allocation$210

Official observations and a separate hypothetical budget. The first two charts use five selected CMAs and two-bedroom apartment averages for Q2 2026, released 9 September 2026. Asking and paid rent describe different populations and unadjusted unit mixes; their difference is not a matched tenant’s rent increase or a pure inflation rate. Data are experimental, in current CAD and subject to revision. The budget charts use only the independently entered rent quote and costs. No city average automatically becomes your quote. The monthly budget excludes deposits, moving costs, income tax calculations and credit or landlord qualification. A negative residual needs a funding or spending change.

The central idea

An average asking rent, an existing tenant’s payment and your own quote answer different questions. Use the statistics for context and the actual option for the cash plan.

01

Identify the quarter, unit type and rental population

The first chart uses Statistics Canada’s Q2 2026 rent comparison, released on 9 September 2026. It shows two-bedroom apartments in five selected census metropolitan areas. Amounts are monthly current Canadian dollars.

Asking rent comes from advertised rental listings. Paid rent describes amounts paid by existing renter households. These are different populations, with potentially different apartment characteristics and inclusions. The experimental estimates are subject to revision.

The five locations were selected to show several relationships between the measures. They are not a complete ranking of Canadian rental markets, a sample of equivalent apartments or evidence that a particular household should relocate. A CMA also covers a broader area than a single neighbourhood.

02

A difference between averages is not a tenant’s rent increase

For Vancouver, the displayed asking and paid averages are CAD 3,030 and CAD 2,470. Subtracting gives CAD 560. Toronto’s corresponding difference is CAD 490, from CAD 2,650 less CAD 2,160.

The relationship is not positive everywhere. Calgary’s asking average of CAD 1,890 is CAD 40 below its paid average of CAD 1,930. Edmonton’s two figures are both CAD 1,570. Regina’s asking average is CAD 100 lower than its paid average. The signed bars make those directions explicit.

These subtractions compare groups in the same quarter. They do not follow one tenant from an old apartment into a matched new apartment. They therefore cannot establish what a particular move, renewal or rent increase will cost. Statistics Canada’s release also distinguishes these rent levels from the CPI rent index’s price-change concept.

03

Replace the average with the option you can actually rent

The budget tool has its own rent-quote input. It does not choose a city average for you. The default uses CAD 2,400 rent, CAD 150 utilities outside that rent, CAD 40 tenant insurance and CAD 200 transport for the location.

Rent, utilities and tenant insurance total CAD 2,590 a month. Adding transport brings the location-related cash requirement to CAD 2,790. Whether the amount is workable then depends on income and every other commitment, rather than on the rent number alone.

Check what the quote includes. If heating, parking or another service is already included, do not add the same amount again outside rent. Conversely, a lower advertised rent can come with separate costs. Compare actual inclusions and travel requirements before interpreting an apparent price difference.

04

Keep saving and other living costs in the reconciliation

With CAD 5,500 monthly take-home income, CAD 2,790 of location-related costs, CAD 2,000 of other living expenses and a CAD 500 saving allocation, the default leaves CAD 210 unassigned each month. The waterfall makes every subtraction visible.

The saving allocation remains a household asset, but it is committed cash in this plan. Omitting it would change the question from whether the option supports the selected goals to whether it covers current consumption alone. A negative residual requires a funding source or a change in commitments.

This is a take-home cash budget. It is not a formal landlord, mortgage, benefit or statistical affordability test, and it does not apply a universal percentage threshold. Moving deposits and overlapping rents belong in a separate dated transition plan, rather than being hidden inside a recurring monthly average.

05

Use the income-and-quote matrix to test the margin

The matrix replaces net household income and the actual rent quote. Utilities, insurance, transport, other living expenses and saving remain selected. Every cell reports the monthly amount left after those commitments.

Negative cells show a shortfall. A small positive amount should also prompt a review of omitted or irregular expenses. The matrix has no probability model, and the official city averages are not used inside it. It is a deterministic check of the amounts entered.

  1. Use the statistics to understand their defined market and period.
  2. Obtain a real quote and a clear list of inclusions.
  3. Build a complete recurring budget from net income.
  4. Fund deposits, moving costs and overlap on their actual dates.
  5. Recheck the plan when the quote, income or household changes.

Keep the original observation date beside any cited statistic. A newly retrieved historical table is still a historical observation, not a current offer available to the household.

Sources and scope

Public sources reviewed on 25 October 2026. The first chart shows ten official rent observations. The second subtracts those observed levels. The last two use independently entered hypothetical budget amounts, without automatically substituting a city average for a rent quote. Original scenario calculations and research checklists are TickerLantern’s educational analysis; attributed publisher examples retain their stated source and scope. Recheck current issuer documents for any product-specific decision.

  1. Statistics Canada · Q2 2026 asking and paid rent comparison · Chart 1 ↗

    Table 46-10-0092-01; released 9 September 2026, reviewed 25 October 2026. Ten monthly current-CAD observations for two-bedroom apartments in five selected CMAs were verified against the accessible HTML table. No suppressed or unavailable paid-rent cells are treated as zero.

  2. Statistics Canada · Quarterly rent statistics, second quarter 2026 ↗

    Definitions, differing rental populations, unit-mix limitations and experimental/revision status. The source does not validate the independent rent quote, household budget, relocation choice or future rent growth.
